blocks.text: The phone in your pocket does not count the way you do. It has only two digits, 0 and 1, yet it stores every song and every photo you own. Number bases explain how that is possible — and WAEC asks about them almost every year.

blocks.markdown:
We normally count in **base ten** because we have ten fingers. In base ten there are ten digits, $0$ to $9$, and each place is worth ten times the place to its right: units, tens, hundreds, thousands.

A **base** is simply the size of the grouping. In base five you group in fives, so the places are worth $1, 5, 25, 125, \dots$ and the only digits allowed are $0, 1, 2, 3, 4$.

blocks.title: The digits available in base n
blocks.text: In base $n$ the digits run from $0$ to $n - 1$. So base 2 uses only 0 and 1, base 5 uses 0 to 4, and base 8 uses 0 to 7. A numeral containing the digit 5 can never be a base 5 number.

blocks.caption: Expanding a base five numeral using place value

blocks.title: Converting to base ten
blocks.prompt: Convert 324 in base 5 to base ten.

steps.text: Write the place value of each column, starting from 0 on the right.
Multiply each digit by its place value.

blocks.answer: 324 in base 5 equals 89 in base ten

blocks.markdown:
### Going the other way

To convert **from** base ten **to** another base, divide repeatedly by the new base and keep the remainders. The remainders, read **from bottom to top**, give the answer.

This works because each division strips off one place value at a time.

blocks.title: Converting from base ten
blocks.prompt: Convert 45 from base ten to base 2.

steps.text: Divide 45 by 2 and record the remainder.
Read the remainders upwards, from the last one to the first.

blocks.answer: 45 in base ten equals 101101 in base 2

blocks.caption: The same quantity written in four different bases

blocks.markdown:
### Adding and subtracting in a base

The column method still works — only the carrying changes. In base 5 you carry when a column reaches **5**, not 10.

For $23_5 + 14_5$: the units give $3 + 4 = 7$. Since $7 = 5 + 2$, write $2$ and carry $1$. The next column gives $2 + 1 + 1 = 4$. So the answer is $42_5$.

When subtracting, a borrow is worth the size of the base. Borrowing in base 5 adds **5** to the column, not 10.

blocks.title: Equations with an unknown base
blocks.text: Questions like "find $x$ if $34_x = 28_{10}$" are common in JAMB. Expand the left side using place value to get $3x + 4 = 28$, then solve normally. Always reject any answer where a digit in the numeral is greater than or equal to your $x$.

points: In base $n$ the place values are powers of $n$ and the digits run from 0 to $n - 1$.
Convert to base ten by multiplying each digit by its place value and adding.
Convert from base ten by dividing repeatedly by the new base and reading remainders upwards.
Column addition and subtraction still work, but you carry and borrow in groups of the base.
For an unknown base, expand using place value to form an equation and solve it.
